# Parkinson disease

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Neurology > Neurocognitive disorders > Parkinson disease*

[Original Article Link](/library/C30qkf)

---

## Summary

Parkinson disease (PD) is a <u>neurodegenerative condition</u> that involves the progressive depletion of <u>dopaminergic</u> <u>neurons</u> in the <u>basal ganglia</u>, particularly the <u>substantia nigra</u>. The disease most commonly manifests at approx. 60 years of age. PD is predominantly considered an <u>idiopathic</u> disease but genetic factors play a role in approx. 10–15% of cases and, accordingly, familial <u>clustering</u> has been observed. A core clinical feature of PD is <u>parkinsonism</u>, a syndrome that comprises <u>bradykinesia</u> along with <u>resting tremor</u> and/or rigidity. <u>Postural instability</u> is a common finding in later stages of PD. <u>Parkinsonism</u> that results from medication, intoxication, or <u>traumatic brain injury</u> is referred to as <u>secondary parkinsonism</u>. <u>Parkinsonism</u> due to <u>neurodegenerative disorders</u> other than PD is called <u>atypical parkinsonism</u> and manifests with features that are not characteristic of PD, such as <u>vertical gaze palsy</u> in <u>progressive supranuclear palsy</u> and <u>apraxia</u> and <u>agnosia</u> in <u>corticobasal degeneration</u>. The diagnosis is clinical; diagnostic testing may be considered to rule out alternative diagnoses. There is currently no cure for PD. Symptomatic treatment includes <u>physical therapy</u> and, depending on patient factors and individual symptoms, certain medications (e.g., <u>levodopa</u>, <u>dopamine agonists</u>). <u>Deep brain stimulation</u> <u>surgery</u> may be beneficial in specific cases.




![Parkinson disease fact sheet](media/lod3inp2jb1cxpfmgkyu526f.jpg)

Parkinson disease fact sheet

## Epidemiology

* <u>Prevalence</u>: second most common <u>neurodegenerative disorder</u> following <u>Alzheimer disease</u> [[1]](/library/viaAt4)

* Age of onset: ∼ 60 years in sporadic cases  [[2]](/library/Eia8t4)

* <u>Risk factors</u>

* Genetic factors: 10–15% of all cases are familial.  [[3]](/library/TYa6oQ)

* Environmental factors (e.g., exposure to <u>manganese</u> and other substances)

* Diet/metabolism (e.g., low levels of <u>vitamin D</u>, high <u>iron</u> intake, <u>obesity</u>)

* History of <u>traumatic brain injury</u>




Epidemiological data refers to the US, unless otherwise specified.

---

## Etiology

### Parkinson disease




* <u>Idiopathic</u>

* Contributing genetic factors include:

* α-Synuclein (SNCA)

* <u>Glucocerebrosidase</u> (GBA): A mutation in the GBA <u>gene</u> (the same <u>gene</u> associated with <u>Gaucher disease</u>) is the most common genetic <u>risk factor</u> for PD.  GBA mutations are associated with altered <u>autophagy</u> and <u>lysosomal</u> function, potentially resulting in impairment of α-synuclein clearance.

* Dardarin (LRRK2): A mutation in LRRK2 <u>gene</u> is the most common cause of dominantly inherited PD.

* Parkin (<u>PARK2</u>): A mutation in <u>PARK2</u> <u>gene</u> is the most common cause of recessively inherited PD.





### Secondary parkinsonism




* Medication (<u>drug-induced parkinsonism</u> or pseudoparkinsonism)

* Most frequent cause of <u>secondary parkinsonism</u> [[3]](/library/TYa6oQ)

* Frequent use of drugs with considerable antidopaminergic effects: <u>typical antipsychotics</u> (e.g., <u>haloperidol</u>), some <u>antiemetics</u> (e.g., <u>metoclopramide</u>), some <u>calcium channel blockers</u> (e.g., <u>flunarizine</u>), <u>amiodarone</u>, <u>valproate</u>, and <u>lithium</u> [[3]](/library/TYa6oQ)[[4]](/library/9iaNF4)

* MPTP: an illegal drug that metabolizes to MPP<sup>+</sup>, damaging the <u>substantia nigra</u>

* Metabolic disorders: e.g., <u>Wilson disease</u>, <u>hemochromatosis</u>, <u>Niemann-Pick disease</u>

* Toxins: e.g., <u>manganese</u>, <u>carbon monoxide</u>, carbon disulfide

* <u>Cerebrovascular disease</u> (vascular <u>parkinsonism</u>): <u>subcortical arteriosclerotic encephalopathy</u>

* <u>CNS</u> infections

* <u>Viruses</u>: e.g., <u>herpes simplex virus</u>, <u>human immunodeficiency virus</u>

* Bacteria: e.g., <u>Treponema pallidum</u>, <u>Mycobacterium tuberculosis</u>

* <u>Protozoa</u>: e.g., <u>Toxoplasma gondii</u>, <u>Plasmodium</u> spp.

* <u>Prion</u> agents: <u>Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease</u>

* <u>Atypical parkinsonism</u>: depends on the underlying disease (e.g., genetic abnormalities in <u>Huntington disease</u>)

---

## Pathophysiology

* Progressive <u>dopaminergic</u> <u>neuron</u> degeneration in the <u>substantia nigra</u> (part of the <u>basal ganglia</u>) and the <u>locus coeruleus</u> → <u>dopamine</u> deficiency at the respective <u>receptors</u> of the <u>striatum</u> with interrupted transmission to the <u>thalamus</u> and motor cortex → motor symptoms of PD  [[5]](/library/l5Yv4p)

* <u>Indirect pathway of the basal ganglia</u> is affected (see “<u>Basal ganglia</u>” in “<u>The cerebral cortex, meninges, basal ganglia, and ventricular system</u>”)

* <u>Serotonin</u> and <u>noradrenaline</u> depletion (in the <u>raphe nuclei</u>): likely cause of depressive symptoms

* <u>Acetylcholine</u> surplus (in the <u>nucleus basalis of Meynert</u>): likely cause of <u>dyskinesia</u>





References:[[3]](/library/TYa6oQ)[[5]](/library/l5Yv4p)

---

## Clinical features

### Overview




* Signs of PD gradually progress over time: The course is usually > 10 years.

* Motor signs are unilateral at onset but may progress to the <u>contralateral</u> side.

* Motor signs are asymmetrical (i.e., more pronounced on one side than on another).

* Preclinical (<u>prodromal</u>) stage with nonmotor signs may precede the onset of motor signs (clinical phase).





### Preclinical stage [[6]](/library/zFYrkI)




* <u>Constipation</u>

* <u>Anosmia</u>

* <u>Sleep</u> disturbances

* <u>REM sleep behavior disorder</u> (<u>RBD</u>)

* <u>Restless leg syndrome</u>

* <u>Excessive daytime sleepiness</u>

* <u>Mood disorders</u> (most commonly <u>depression</u>, <u>apathy</u>, and/or <u>anxiety</u>)





### Clinical stage




#### Motor signs [[7]](/library/LgYwDo)




* Parkinsonism: a syndrome comprising <u>bradykinesia</u> and either <u>resting tremor</u> or rigidity (or both) and that is consistent with impairment of the <u>extrapyramidal system</u>

* A core feature of PD

* Can be also seen in a variety of other disorders, e.g., <u>multiple system atrophy</u>, <u>corticobasal degeneration</u> (see “<u>Atypical parkinsonism</u>”)

* Bradykinesia: slowed movements in combination with decreased amplitude/speed when moving

* <u>Resting tremor</u> (4–6 Hz)

* Oftentimes the presenting symptom

* <u>Pill-rolling tremor</u> that subsides with voluntary movements but increases with <u>stress</u>

* Most common in the hands but may involve the legs, <u>jaw</u>, <u>lips</u>, and <u>tongue</u>

* Rigidity: increased and persistent resistance to passive <u>joint</u> movement that is independent of speed 

* Froment maneuver: patient is asked to perform repetitive movements in the <u>contralateral</u> extremity (e.g., opening and closing of the left fist if the right side is examined) → subclinical rigidity becomes more pronounced and may be detected

* Cogwheel rigidity

* A phenomenon caused by the overlay of increased muscle <u>tonus</u> and <u>resting tremor</u> in patients with PD

* May manifest before <u>tremor</u> becomes clinically apparent

* Muscles in an extremity (most commonly the arms) are passively stretched, eliciting a jerking-like motion.

* Muscle tone should be tested with at least two <u>joints</u>.

* Postural instability  

* Imbalance and tendency to fall

* Evaluated with the pull test

* Gait abnormalities

* Parkinsonian gait: shuffling gait with quickened and shortened steps

* <u>Freezing</u>: sudden inability to start or continue movements

* Festination: gait pattern characterized by small, increasingly quick steps

* Propulsion: forward-leaning gait with a risk of a patient falling forward

* Decreased arm swing

* Other motor findings

* Unhabituated <u>glabellar reflex</u>

* Signs of <u>dystonia</u>

* Stooped posture

* Abnormal <u>flexor posturing</u> of hands and feet (i.e., striatal deformities)

* Micrographia: size of handwriting is reduced

* Hypomimia: low degree of facial expression





> [!TIP]
> <u>Parkinsonism</u> is required for the diagnosis of Parkinson disease. Unilateral onset is characteristic of Parkinson disease.




> [!NOTE]
> <u>Parkinsonism</u> <u>TRAP</u>s the patient: Tremor, Rigidity, Akinesia, and Postural instability.




#### Nonmotor signs




* Autonomic symptoms 

* <u>Orthostatic hypotension</u>

* Oily <u>skin</u>

* <u>Urinary urgency</u>

* Impaired sexual function

* Neuropsychiatric symptoms

* <u>Depression</u>

* Cognitive problems, e.g., decreased attention and concentration, executive dysfunction, impaired <u>memory</u> (Parkinson dementia): develop in advanced disease  [[5]](/library/l5Yv4p)

* <u>Apathy</u>

* Behavioral changes (e.g., irritability, impulsivity)

* <u>Disordered sleep</u> (<u>sleep</u> fragmentation; , vivid dreams)

* Fatigue

* <u>Hyposmia</u>, <u>anosmia</u>

## Diagnosis

### Approach [[8]](/library/fS1k_T0)[[9]](/library/TS16_T0)[[10]](/library/3S1SzT0)




* Consider PD in patients with <u>parkinsonism</u>.

* Perform a thorough clinical evaluation.

* Consider diagnostic testing to:

* Provide diagnostic certainty if a diagnosis cannot be made based on clinical features alone

* Help rule out alternative diagnoses of <u>parkinsonism</u>

* Refer to a <u>neurologist</u> or movement disorder specialist for diagnostic confirmation.





> [!TIP]
> Parkinson disease is a <u>clinical diagnosis</u>. A definitive diagnosis requires postmortem confirmation of <u>Lewy bodies</u>.




### Clinical evaluation [[10]](/library/3S1SzT0)[[11]](/library/8iaOt4)




* Evaluate for typical <u>clinical features of PD</u> based on:

* Detailed <u>patient history</u>

* Thorough <u>physical examination</u>, including complete <u>neurological examination</u>

* Assess for:

* Supportive features of PD

* Atypical features for PD suggesting other causes of <u>parkinsonism</u>

* A diagnosis can be made by a specialist using diagnostic criteria (see “Tips and Links”).





#### Supportive features [[11]](/library/8iaOt4)




* A diagnosis of PD requires the presence of <u>parkinsonism</u> (i.e., <u>bradykinesia</u> and either <u>resting tremor</u>, rigidity, or both).

* Supportive features include:

* Clear benefit from <u>dopaminergic</u> medication  [[12]](/library/xe1EaT0)

* <u>Resting tremor</u>

* <u>Levodopa</u>-induced <u>dyskinesia</u> (typically occurs during later stages of PD)

* Olfactory loss





#### Atypical features




Consider other causes of <u>parkinsonism</u> if any of the following are present :




* Features

* <u>Vertical gaze palsy</u>

* <u>Cortical signs</u>

* <u>Cerebellar signs</u>

* <u>Pyramidal tract signs</u>

* Absence of typical nonmotor signs

* Disease trajectory 

* Rapid progression (e.g., early <u>dementia</u>, progressive <u>aphasia</u>, falls, gait impairment, severe autonomic or <u>bulbar dysfunction</u>)

* No progression of typical motor signs

* No benefit from <u>dopaminergic</u> medication

* Distribution of symptoms

* Bilateral symmetric <u>parkinsonism</u>

* Limited to legs

* History suggestive of alternative causes

* Use of <u>dopaminergic</u> blockers within 6–12 months

* <u>Traumatic brain injury</u>

* <u>Encephalitis</u>





> [!TIP]
> If patients have atypical features for PD, evaluate for <u>secondary parkinsonism</u> or <u>atypical parkinsonian syndromes</u>.




### Diagnostic testing




#### Imaging [[13]](/library/Ge1BZT0) [[14]](/library/UQabv4)




Imaging is not routinely required for diagnosis but can be considered under specialist guidance if the diagnosis is unclear.




* <u>MRI</u> <u>brain</u>: usually no specific changes, nonspecific <u>atrophy</u> of the <u>putamen</u> may be seen in patients with PD

* DaTSCAN: <u>SPECT</u> with visualization of striatal <u>dopamine</u> transporters using <sup>123</sup>I-ioflupane

* Syndromes with <u>nigrostriatal</u> degeneration (e.g., PD, <u>MSA</u>): reduced <u>dopamine</u> transporter activity

* <u>Essential tremor</u>: normal

* Iodobenzamide single-photon emission computed tomography (<u>IBZM-SPECT</u>): measures <u>D2-receptor</u> density in the <u>striatum</u>  [[15]](/library/fQakv4)

* PD: normal or increased <u>D2-receptor</u> density

* <u>Atypical parkinsonism</u>: decreased <u>D2-receptor</u> density

* Other modalities (rarely used)

* PET

* Transcranial <u>sonography</u>





#### Ancillary tests




Ancillary tests are not routinely used but can support the diagnosis.




* Levodopa challenge test: performed to support the diagnosis of PD or as part of the evaluation prior to implantation of a deep <u>brain</u> stimulator

* Motor symptoms are evaluated before, during, and after administration of oral <u>levodopa</u> and a <u>decarboxylase inhibitor</u>.

* The result is positive if administration of <u>levodopa</u> relieves symptoms.

* Olfactory testing: to test for <u>hyposmia</u>  [[8]](/library/fS1k_T0)[[9]](/library/TS16_T0)[[16]](/library/ze1rYT0)[[17]](/library/b21HTT0)

* MIBG <u>myocardial</u> <u>scintigraphy</u>: to test for cardiac <u>sympathetic denervation</u>

## Pathology

* <u>Lewy bodies</u>

* Aggregates of misfolded α-synuclein and other <u>proteins</u>, such as <u>ubiquitin</u> and <u>neurofilament</u> protein within the neural cell bodies

* Appear histologically as intracellular <u>hyaline</u> eosinophilic globules

* May be found in <u>brainstem</u>, <u>substantia nigra</u>, and cortex  [[6]](/library/zFYrkI)

* Also seen in <u>dementia with Lewy bodies</u>

* Loss of <u>dopaminergic</u> <u>neurons</u> in <u>substantia nigra</u> pars compacta, causing depigmentation of <u>substantia nigra</u> on gross and microscopic examination

* <u>Reactive gliosis</u> is found within the areas of neural degeneration. [[5]](/library/l5Yv4p)

## Management

### General principles  [[13]](/library/Ge1BZT0)[[17]](/library/b21HTT0)[[22]](/library/xU1E2T0)




* Offer <u>supportive care</u> to all patients.

* Initiate pharmacotherapy when symptoms start to cause functional impairment.

* Consult a <u>neurologist</u> or movement disorder specialist before initiating or changing treatment.

* Manage associated symptoms (e.g., <u>major depressive disorder</u>, <u>dementia</u>) as necessary.





> [!TIP]
> Pharmacotherapy does not alter the disease trajectory in PD; initiate when symptoms interfere with quality of life.




### <u>Supportive care</u> [[10]](/library/3S1SzT0)




* <u>Rehabilitation</u>

* <u>Physical therapy</u> and exercise

* <u>Occupational therapy</u>

* <u>Speech therapy</u>

* Fall prevention  [[23]](/library/X219TT0)

* Assess for and eliminate or treat <u>risk factors</u>.

* See “<u>Falls in older adults</u>.”

* Nutrition

* Encourage fiber intake and adequate hydration to reduce <u>constipation</u>.

* Ensure adequate <u>calcium</u> and <u>vitamin D</u> intake to <u>optimize bone health</u>.

* Consider referral to a dietitian for specialist advice.

* <u>Sleep hygiene</u>

* <u>Advance care planning</u>

* Prognosis and end-of-life choices should be discussed early.

* Consider <u>palliative care</u> as needed.





### Treatment [[10]](/library/3S1SzT0)[[24]](/library/Pq1WA30)[[25]](/library/jI1_cR0)




Choose initial therapy based on individual patient factors (e.g., motor symptoms, age, comorbidities). To delay <u>levodopa</u>-based treatment for as long as possible, various age thresholds were previously recommended.  [[25]](/library/jI1_cR0)




* Commonly used options for initial monotherapy include <u>levodopa</u>, a <u>dopamine agonist</u>, or an <u>MAO-B inhibitor</u>.

* Risk factors for levodopa-induced dyskinesia include: [[24]](/library/Pq1WA30)

* Young age

* Low body weight

* Female sex

* Severe disease

* In patients with refractory symptoms or intolerable adverse effects that require dose reduction, consider:

* Switching monotherapy

* Combination therapy

* Avoid abrupt discontinuation or sudden changes in medication.

* Consider enteral infusion of <u>levodopa</u> or <u>deep brain stimulation</u> for patients with advanced disease and severe motor fluctuations.

* See “<u>Medication for Parkinson disease</u>” for additional information on mechanisms of action and adverse effects.





> [!TIP]
> <u>Levodopa</u> is the most effective treatment for motor symptoms in PD but is associated with time- and dosage-dependent increase of <u>dyskinesia</u>.




> [!WARNING]
> Avoid abrupt discontinuation or sudden changes in medication. Consult a specialist if such changes are necessary.

[[24]](/library/Pq1WA30)<br><br> | <br>* Compared to <u>levodopa</u>:<br><br>* Less effective for motor symptoms<br><br>* Higher risk of psychiatric adverse effects, e.g., <u>impulse control disorders</u>, confusion, <u>hallucinations</u><br><br> |
| <u>MAO-B inhibitors</u> | <br>* <u>Selegiline</u> DOSAGE<br><br> | <br>* May be trialed as initial therapy for mild disease in patients with <u>bradykinesia</u> or <u>postural instability</u><br><br> | <br><br>* May improve <u>end-of-dose akinesia</u><br><br>* May worsen <u>dyskinesias</u><br><br><br> |
| <u>Anticholinergics</u> | <br><br>* <u>Benztropine</u> DOSAGE [[22]](/library/xU1E2T0)<br><br>* <u>Trihexyphenidyl</u> DOSAGE [[22]](/library/xU1E2T0)<br><br><br> | <br>* Consider as initial treatment for younger patients in whom <u>tremor</u> is the <u>chief concern</u>.<br><br> | <br>* May cause <u>anticholinergic effects</u>, e.g., psychiatric symptoms or <u>urinary retention</u> (especially in older adults)<br><br> |
| <u>NMDA antagonist</u> | <br>* <u>Amantadine</u> DOSAGE<br><br> | <br><br>* Short-term treatment of mild symptoms<br><br>* <u>Levodopa</u>-induced <u>dyskinesia</u><br><br>* <u>Akinetic crisis</u><br><br><br> | <br>* May cause adverse <u>CNS</u> effects, e.g.:<br><br>* <u>Delirium</u><br><br>* <u>Dizziness</u><br><br>* <u>Anxiety</u><br><br> |
| <u>COMT inhibitors</u> | <br>* <u>Entacapone</u> DOSAGE<br><br> | <br>* <u>End-of-dose akinesia</u><br><br> | <br>* Used only in combination with <u>carbidopa/levodopa</u><br><br> |





> [!WARNING]
> <u>Anticholinergics</u> and <u>levodopa</u>/<u>carbidopa</u> can increase <u>intraocular pressure</u>; avoid in patients with <u>glaucoma</u>.




> [!TIP]
> <u>Ergot</u> <u>dopamine agonists</u> (e.g., <u>bromocriptine</u>) have mostly been replaced by <u>nonergot</u> <u>agonists</u> because of significant side effects (e.g., <u>pulmonary fibrosis</u>).




> [!WARNING]
> Overstimulation of <u>D2 receptors</u> by <u>levodopa</u> or <u>dopamine agonists</u> may induce <u>psychosis</u> and <u>hallucinations</u>, especially in older patients with concurrent <u>dementia</u> or other psychiatric disorders.

Mechanism of action: drugs used in Parkinson disease




#### Deep brain stimulation (<u>DBS</u>)   [[13]](/library/Ge1BZT0)[[26]](/library/kQamw4)




* Indications

* Severe motor symptoms or refractory <u>tremor</u>

* Decrease in dosage of medication because of adverse effects

* Procedure

* Stereotactic implantation of stimulating electrode(s) targeting the <u>subthalamic nucleus</u> or internal <u>globus pallidus</u>

* Controlled remotely

* Complications

* Infection

* Hemorrhage

* Breakage or displacement of electrodes or leads





![Deep brain stimulation](media/jnna2ldihmyb1e518jtw795a.jpg)

Deep brain stimulation




### Treatment of associated symptoms [[13]](/library/Ge1BZT0)[[22]](/library/xU1E2T0)




Under specialist guidance, carefully consider the risks and benefits of pharmacological treatment of nonmotor symptoms.




* <u>Major depressive disorder</u>

* Options include <u>cognitive behavioral therapy</u> and/or treatment with an <u>antidepressant</u>, e.g., <u>SSRI</u>, <u>SNRI</u>, or <u>tricyclic antidepressant</u>.

* Do not combine these drug classes with <u>MAO-B inhibitors</u>.

* <u>Dementia</u>: Consider treatment with <u>rivastigmine</u>.

* <u>Psychosis</u>

* Taper off <u>antiparkinson medications</u> as able.

* Consider <u>pimavanserin</u>, <u>clozapine</u>, or <u>quetiapine</u> (<u>off-label</u>).  [[13]](/library/Ge1BZT0)

* <u>Autonomic dysfunction</u> [[10]](/library/3S1SzT0)

* <u>Detrusor</u> hyperactivity: Consider medications without significant <u>CNS</u> effects when available (e.g., <u>trospium chloride</u>).

* <u>Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension</u>: Consider <u>droxidopa</u>.

* <u>Constipation</u>

* Encourage <u>lifestyle changes for constipation</u>.

* Consider <u>polyethylene glycol</u> or <u>probiotic therapy</u>.

* <u>Erectile dysfunction</u>: Consider <u>sildenafil</u>.

* <u>Sialorrhea</u>: Options include <u>botulinum toxin</u> injections, <u>glycopyrrolate</u>, or sublingual <u>atropine</u>.

* <u>Sleep disorders</u> (e.g., <u>RBD</u>)

* Consider treatment with <u>melatonin</u> or <u>clonazepam</u>.

* Improve <u>sleep hygiene</u>.





> [!WARNING]
> While improvement of nonmotor symptoms is often crucial for quality of life, treatments often worsen other <u>clinical features of PD</u>.
